Adolescent Kyphosis: Does the Curve Correct?

Run the correction test before naming it postural or Scheuermann

DiagnosisManagementPractice
Bottom line

A teenager with thoracic roundback: lie the patient prone or ask for active extension.

  • Corrects fully: postural kyphosis. Exercises and reassurance; a film, if taken, shows a smooth curve without wedging.
  • Stays rigid, often with activity-related mid-back pain: standing lateral film. Wedging of 5 degrees or more in 3 or more consecutive vertebrae is Scheuermann disease, most often in boys aged 12 to 17.

Treat by curve size and growth: observe and exercise a mild curve; brace a moderate curve (about 50 to 75 degrees; one source gives 60 to 80) or one that progresses, while growth remains; fuse a severe curve (over about 75 degrees) or refractory pain, even with growth remaining.

Diagnosis
Defining findings Rigid – over 40 degrees (normal 20 to 40); does not correct prone or in extension · Film – anterior wedging of 5 degrees or more in 3 or more consecutive vertebrae (Sorensen) · Schmorl nodes – disc herniation through the endplate; dramatic on film, not an emergency; support, not required
Mimics Compression fracture – trauma or osteoporosis; acute focal pain; height loss at one level, not three · Ankylosing spondylitis – young adult; sacroiliac pain, morning stiffness; not isolated thoracic wedging
Management and treatment
Management ladder: Scheuermann kyphosis
TierInterventionEscalate when
Mild curveObserve; exercise and stretchingCurve reaches the brace range or progresses, growth remaining
Moderate or progressing, still growingBrace until skeletal maturity; it halts progression, rarely correctsSevere curve (over about 75 degrees) or refractory pain
Severe or refractory painPosterior spinal fusionTop rung
Practice
  1. 17-year-old boy with 1 year of worsening thoracic roundback aching mid-back pain curve does not correct prone or in extension No morning stiffness or buttock pain Afebrile · lateral film: 8-degree anterior wedging of 3 consecutive mid-thoracic vertebrae, Schmorl nodes → Scheuermann disease → a rigid kyphosis with 5 degrees or more of wedging in 3 consecutive vertebrae is Scheuermann disease; Schmorl nodes support it
  2. 15-year-old girl whose parents worry about her posture round shoulders for 2 years curve fully corrects lying prone and on active extension No back pain Afebrile · lateral film: smooth curve, no vertebral wedging → Postural kyphosis → a curve that fully corrects is postural kyphosis, the most common cause of adolescent roundback: postural exercises and reassurance; no structural vertebral change
  3. 16-year-old boy with 8 months of increasing thoracic roundback mild mid-back ache after sports curve does not correct in hyperextension No pain that wakes him from sleep or weight loss Afebrile · neurologic exam normal → Standing lateral thoracic spine radiograph → a rigid kyphosis gets a standing lateral spine film first to measure the wedging and the Cobb angle; MRI is for pain that wakes from sleep, weight loss or neurologic signs
  4. 14-year-old boy was diagnosed with Scheuermann disease 1 year ago Cobb angle now 65 degrees, up from 52 about 2 years of growth remaining Doing his extension exercises Afebrile · neurologic exam normal → Brace until skeletal maturity → a 65-degree curve sits in the brace range and is progressing; with growth remaining it is braced to halt progression until maturity; fusion is for a severe curve, over about 75 degrees, or refractory pain
  5. 17-year-old boy was diagnosed with Scheuermann disease at 13 Cobb angle 80 degrees skeletally mature; physes closed on film Back pain limits school despite a year of physical therapy Afebrile · neurologic exam normal → Posterior spinal fusion → a severe curve (over about 75 degrees) or refractory pain at skeletal maturity goes to posterior spinal fusion; a brace no longer works once growth ends
Transferable rule

One bedside maneuver, whether the curve corrects, separates structural from postural kyphosis; the film confirms, it does not decide.
